column5: Coverage rules: master first, then two-shot, OTS and close-ups; answering shots should match focal length, focus distance, lens height and horizontal angle; the book allows judged exceptions for actors of different heights.

Shooting methods: master scene, plan scene (one choreographed shot), overlapping/run-and-gun for industrials and events. Touch of Evil's opening (about 3 1/4 minutes, one crane shot) keeps a ticking bomb in tension throughout.
Hitchcock's rule as the book gives it: the size of an object in frame should equal its importance in the story at that moment. Cites Touch of Evil and From Shanghai.
Window and door matching, turnaround cheating and eyeline marks are standard cheats. The book says the camera operator, who sees through the lens, has the final say on whether a cheat shows.

Composition rules the book gives: rule of thirds as a starting point; keep key elements inside TV Safe (about 10% in from the frame edge); headroom as little as the frame allows; noseroom because a turned head has visual weight.
Frame edges and off-screen space carry visual force; the book says to avoid cutting people off at the ankles or wrists in static shots.
The book says atmospheric perspective can be faked with a fine net in front of translights or backdrops, reducing detail so they look farther away.

Lens perspective: wide lenses exaggerate depth and give a sense of presence; long lenses compress space and flatten movement toward the camera. Normal lens is roughly the diagonal of the frame; the book says about 40mm on 35mm film fits typical vision.

Focus rules of thumb given: focus goes to the person speaking (racks allowed in dialogue), to the person facing camera or most prominent, then to the person in the most emotional moment. When in doubt, the lower call-sheet number. Rack focus must be rehearsed.

The book says depth of field is inversely proportional to the square of focal length. That holds only at a fixed subject distance and image size, so the course should not state it as a general rule without that condition.
Kubrick's Barry Lyndon and Jarmusch's Stranger Than Paradise use fixed, static frames for their meaning. Hitchcock's principle (object size = story importance) is applied again to Lady from Shanghai.

Shutter angle: 180 degrees is standard, so each frame at 24 fps is exposed about 1/48 s (the OCR reads 1/50th). A 90 degree shutter gives a sharper moving image; narrower angles give a strobing effect.

Low-speed blur: shooting at 6 or 12 fps with a long exposure makes action look slowed down while it runs at normal speed. Useful for commercials; the book gives this as a known effect, not a camera setting.

Lens height: eye level is default for dialogue. High angles reveal layout and reduce the subject; low angles raise its power. Hitchcock's bomb-under-the-table example makes the point that suspense needs the audience to know more than the characters.
Dutch tilt and reveals as motivated tools. Shots that track past walls need a hidden cut or a vertical edge to hide the camera's passage.

Pan speed rule of thumb in the book: at 180 degrees and 24-25 fps an object should take at least 5 seconds to cross the frame, or strobing shows. This is the book's own rule; the course should give it as a guideline and not as a measured figure.

Motivation and settling: a camera move should start and end with purpose and settle for a beat before a cut. Zoom versus dolly: a zoom keeps the viewpoint and changes perspective and depth of field; a dolly changes the background behind the subject. Zoom in while dollying out keeps image size and changes perspective (Jaws, Goodfellas).

Rig vocabulary for the course's moves: dolly in/out, crab, track, boom, crane, remote head, Steadicam, hostess tray and hood mount for car shots, camera-car towing. Book notes that crane and camera-car accidents are among the industry's leading causes of serious injury and death.

Fluid heads give resistance and are preferred by most operators; geared heads suit repeatable studio moves. A tripod with a high-hat gives low lens height; the book suggests a sandbag, rocker plate or low-mode prism to go lower.

The line (180-degree rule): the camera stays on one side of the action line; the line is established by a look, movement, a specific action, exit from frame, or geography. A neutral shot (moving directly toward or away from camera) can let you cross it. Reverse angles are valid when the crossing is bold and motivated.

The 20% rule: two shots must change by at least about 20% in angle, lens size or position to cut; the 30-degree move on the 180 circle is a specific case. Two lens steps (e.g. 50mm to 25mm) may be needed. Judgment decides.

Editing cut types the book lists: content, action, POV, match, conceptual and zero cut. Zero cut stitches two shots of the same angle and lens; the book cites The Last Boy Scout and Ronin. Action cuts should always overlap the movement.
Rope is described as one long take with a few cuts hidden at reel changes; a roll lasts about 11 minutes. The book calls the claim of no cuts a myth.

The book gives 1 foot-candle as about 10.08 lux. The accepted figure is about 10.76 lux (multiply by 10.76). Any course conversion should use 10.76 and cite the standard; check the book's conversion before quoting it.

Exposure basics: one stop = twice or half the light; third-stop precision is the practical limit; inverse square law: moving a lamp from 11 ft to 8 ft gains one stop. Cosine law: a surface turned away from the light loses exposure in proportion to the cosine of the angle.

The book says film base is 4 to 7 thousandths of an inch (given as 0.025 mm). 0.025 mm is one thousandth of an inch; 4 to 7 thousandths is about 0.10 to 0.18 mm. Do not repeat the book's base thickness without correcting it.
The book dates Kodak's T-grain to the 1970s. T-grain emulsions date from the early 1980s; verify before citing the date.

Zone system for exposure: Zone V is 18% reflectance (middle gray); an incident reading, a spot reading of an 18% card and a Zone V subject should agree. Placement and fall: choose the zone a subject should print at, then light the rest of the scene to fall around it. Use a gray card or palm reading (Zone VI) if no spot is available.

Exposure time with a 180 degree shutter is 1/48 s at 24 fps (rounded to 1/50 s, 1/50 s at 25 fps). Ramping and high or low speed change exposure time; the book's table gives stop shifts by frame rate and shutter angle.

Book cautions: its skin-tone and Zone V examples ('Caucasian skin is Zone VI'; a different starting point for African-American subjects) are rules of thumb of the time. Do not repeat them without qualification; a meter reading on the subject is the better guide.

The book dates Weber's discovery to 1890 and names him as the source of the logarithmic perception law. Weber's work dates from the 1830s; Fechner gave the logarithmic law in 1860. Check any date before citing it.

The book says visible light is produced only when an electron falls into the second shell of an atom. That is too narrow: visible emission comes from many electron transitions, and thermal sources emit across the spectrum. Do not repeat the mechanism.

Colour basics the book gives that suit module 4: light is additive (RGB), paint and film dyes are subtractive (CMY); Purkinje effect explains why night is conventionally lit blue; warm and cool colours shift mood; advancing and retreating colours. Its counts of hues and value steps (about 150 and 200) are unsourced; do not quote them.

Metamerism: paint, wardrobe and set colours that match under one source may not match under another. Judge sets, props and wardrobe under the lighting they will actually meet. Standard sources in the 1931 CIE set: A (2854 K tungsten), B (4800 K noon sun), C (6500 K daylight); 5500 K is still the common lighting-instrument standard.

Light types with the book's cautions: HMIs give more light per watt than tungsten, need a ballast, are rated CRI 90 or above, and flicker-free (square-wave) ballasts matter at non-sync frame rates. Keep HMIs grounded and dry, never run without the lens glass, and check header cables first when one fails to strike.
OCR error: the rare-earth names in the HMI section are garbled (sysporsium, thulium, homium). The chemistry is correct for dysprosium, holmium etc. Verify before quoting.

Equipment for the course's lighting modules: fresnels, PARs and soft lights, with cautions: never point a 5K, 10K or 20K straight up; keep gels away from the light face; colour-correct high-frequency fluorescents (Kino Flo, from 1987 on Barfly) are flicker-free and cooler. Practical bulb sizes are a rental matter; confirm with the rental house.

Lighting as storytelling: light and shadow carry story and character. Examples used: Caravaggio's Calling of St Matthew, film noir low-key lighting shaped by post-war fast film and portable lights, and Deschanel's work in The Natural (silhouette, blue night, lightning as a motif). Book's view: light should motivate the story, not just expose the set.

The book gives 85 (full CTO) as losing about 2/3 stop and CTB as 36% transmission (about 1.5 stops). By the book's own 58% figure, 85 loses about 0.8 stop (log2 of 1/0.58). Quote the stop loss from the filter maker's data sheet, not from the text.

Colour balance practice the course can use: 85 (CTO) on windows and tungsten balance is preferred over full CTB on tungsten lights; mired shift = 1,000,000 / Kelvin, and subtract source from target to get filtration. Fluorescent: take a grey-scale reading before correcting; a CRI of 90 or above is the film threshold.
Unsourced claim: the book says Venice's blue light was made famous by Canaletto. Do not repeat without a source.

Equal framing gives equal depth of field: a wider lens only gains depth of field if the camera is not moved back to keep the same frame. Image magnification drives depth of field. Worked example from the book: 50mm at f/8 with a 0.001 in circle of confusion gives a hyperfocal distance of about 40 ft.

The book says depth of field is calculated from the front nodal point. Standard lens charts measure subject distance from the image (film) plane, and nodal points matter mainly for parallax and close-up work. Check the lens or chart before stating the nodal rule in the course.

Hyperfocal rules confirmed by the book's own maths: opening two stops doubles hyperfocal distance; at hyperfocal the sharp zone runs from half the distance to infinity; focus at a third of the distance for half-hyperfocal. Depth of field is roughly one third in front of the focus point and two thirds behind.

Close-up tools with checkable figures: extension factor squared gives the filter factor (2X = 2 stops, 3X = about 3 stops); exposure at close range: meter f-stop divided by (1 + magnification) with the book's 1:2 example; diopter minimum focus is 100 cm divided by dioptre power; split diopters need a hidden seam. Depth of field depends on image magnification, not focal length alone.

Lens tests the book lists for hire-day checks: resolution, corner resolution, vignetting, focus breathing (optical shift), distortion, collimation, infinity focus, veiling glare, colour consistency and contrast. Useful for the DSLR and lens module's checklist.

Video exposure: the waveform monitor is the reliable meter; keep important picture values between 7.5 and 100 IRE ('legal' video). The vectorscope checks colour. Monitors can mislead, so do not judge exposure from a picture monitor alone. Useful for the DSLR module's exposure section.

The book says digital video has no setup (black level offset). Many digital systems use a setup or a limited-range (16 to 235) encoding, so say 'limited range' or 'depends on the codec' rather than 'no setup'.
Frame-count detail: the book gives NTSC as 525 lines with 481 visible; the usual figure is about 486 visible lines (480 in common use). Check before quoting the number.

Timecode and frame rates, checkable: 29.97 fps drops frame numbers 00 and 01 each minute except every tenth, so an hour of 29.97 video reads as an hour; 24 and 25 fps need no drop frame; slate 5 seconds of pre-roll so timecode locks. Ten minutes of NTSC is 17,982 frames.

The book's 4:2:0 description gives only the sample rates for luma and chroma. The chroma is also halved vertically, so say '4:2:0 halves chroma both horizontally and vertically'. Check the codec's data sheet before quoting.

Telecine prep checklist from the book: shoot a grey scale, confer with the telecine house before any off-speed or green-screen work, write frame rate and day/night on the slate, keep a full camera report, pre-roll sound 5 seconds, and send the editor's needs (keykode, flex file) before transfer. 3:2 pulldown holds alternate frames 1/20 s and 1/30 s, so pans judder.

High Def shooting rules the course can cite: shoot at 23.98 or 29.97 rather than 24 or 30; control highlights; expose on the side of under-exposure; avoid regular video zooms on HD; HD sees into shadows and fine detail, so makeup and set detail show. The book says HD speed is about ISO 320 and that more lights are still needed, since doubling speed is one stop only.

Book's transfer claim: Kodak Gray Card Plus waveform targets of 80, 45 and 20 IRE for the 90, 18 and 3 per cent patches, with other cinematographers using 85, 50 and 15. Check the card's current guidance before using either set.

Grey-card method for transfer: light the card from outside the scene, with a neutral 3200 K (or 5500 K for daylight), no filters or dimmer, and check it with an incident and a spot reading. Shoot the card, then a few seconds of the scene; the card is the neutral reference, the scene shows the intent.

The book's printer-light arithmetic does not agree with itself. It says one printer point adds 0.025 log exposure, so 12 points make one stop (0.30 log E). It then says one light changes density by about 0.07 to 0.1, or 1/6 to 1/7 stop, and three lights make half a stop. By its own 0.025 figure, one point is 1/12 stop and three points are 1/4 stop. Use the lab's own printer data, not these figures.

Flashing and Varicon: pre-flashing raises the inertia point and lowers contrast by lifting shadows more than highlights (Table 13.2). Varicon does this through the lens and can be adjusted between shots; Saving Private Ryan used uncoated lenses for internal flare. Relevant to the analogue-film module's look-control section.

Silver retention (bleach-bypass, ENR, CCE, Skip-bleach): these leave silver in the image, which adds density and cuts saturation. The book says skip-bleach can add about 1.5 stops, so underexpose by half to one stop, and test on the exact lab and stock, since release prints are costly to treat. Cross-processing and printing negative as interpositive raise contrast and saturation.

Filter practice for the course: ND filters (0.3 = 1 stop, 0.6 = 2, 0.9 = 3) combine by adding density; polarisers lose about 1 2/3 to 2 stops and work best about 90 degrees from the sun; use no filter or ND on the sun to avoid double images. ND grads: hard or soft edge matters with focal length.

Filter factor rule for black-and-white: expose for the darkest subject that is the same colour as the filter and let the filter lighten its own colour. Colour filters only change contrast when the scene has colour difference.

Pre-shot checks for film and DSLR work, as the book sets them out: confirm T-stop, focus, frame rate and shutter angle before each take (an old FAST check: focus, aperture, speed, tachometer); the frame rate is easy to change by accident (24 to 23 or 25). Check the gate after each scene. The book says a frame-rate slip of one switch is enough to ruin sync.

Slate and camera report practice: slate with scene, take, roll, day or night, sound or MOS and frame rate; a timecode slate must be jammed daily and whenever it says 'feed me'; avoid tail slates; the camera report carries circles, footage and G/NG/W inventory. Useful for the analogue-film module's workflow section.

Flicker rules the course can use: discharge sources (HMI, fluorescent) flicker when shutter and mains do not match. At 24 fps on 60 Hz mains, 144 degrees gives 1/60 s; on 50 Hz, 172.8 degrees gives 1/50 s. Use crystal-controlled generators, check frequency, and prefer flicker-free ballasts for non-sync speeds. Only certain frame rates are safe with a given shutter (the book's tables 15.1 to 15.3).

Unverified in this chapter: the book says a frequency error can change exposure by about 4 stops. That figure needs a source. Also the declination and agonic-line statements are dated: magnetic north moves, so use current data (for example the World Magnetic Model) rather than these figures.

Monitor and roll-bar practice from the book: a 180 degree shutter at 29.97 fps avoids roll bars for video transfer; for 24 fps sync, use a 144 degree shutter at 23.976 fps (about one-third stop loss, roll bar reduced but not removed). Spot meters underread video monitors, often by a stop or more, so trust Polaroids.

Greenscreen guidance (book, citing Ultimatte and Kino Flo): keep background and foreground lighting matched in direction; keep spill off the subject; shoot a clean plate and a grey scale in neutral light; avoid wide-open lenses, diffusion and smoke; ask the compositor for the exposure target before shooting. Vendor-specific figures (30 IRE separation etc.) are theirs, not general rules.

High-speed arithmetic checked: exposure time = (360 / shutter angle) / frame rate, so 120 degrees at 360 fps gives 1/1080 s; times-normal-speed = frame rate / transfer rate (360 / 24 = 15); screen time = frames exposed / transfer rate (360 fps for 0.5 s gives 7.5 s on screen). The book's typed formulae drop the division sign and read as addition; the examples are right, so quote the examples or write the division out.

Strobe and exposure: a strobe does not change exposure with frame rate, but tungsten does, so set the tungsten to the high-speed value and add the two light readings as light, not f-numbers (two f/5.6 sources give f/4). Also: 96 fps on a 180 degree shutter is about two stops less light than 24 fps.
Dated claim: the book says film still beats high-definition video as a total imaging system on MTF. That was a fair comparison in its time; check current figures before repeating it.

Time-lapse arithmetic the course can check: screen time in frames = event duration in seconds / interval in seconds, so six real hours at one frame per minute gives 360 frames (15 s at 24 fps). The book's Steele chart is a useful lookup; intervalometer exposure must allow for light changes during the shot.

Format facts the analogue-film module can use: Academy aperture came with optical sound in 1932; Super 35 uses the full negative, and a common topline keeps the top of the frame consistent across 2.35 and TV; 3-perf saves about a quarter of stock per frame, and 4-perf is the lab standard, so 3-perf is converted before finishing. Anamorphic: 1.18:1 on negative for 2.35 projection.

The book says anamorphic depth of field is half that of the same image size. Whether it is shallower depends on how the field of view is matched; compare two lens choices at equal framing before stating a rule.
